comparable_reason: The angle is invariant to rotation, reflection and isometric embedding (measured 0.0 rad change from D=2 to D=1600), so width does not mechanically set it, and it is now exactly scale-free. But it is a function of the SAMPLING of the trajectory, not only of its shape: the same circle read at 6 vs 60 points gives 72.000 vs 6.102 degrees in BLME and in the released code alike, so cross-model comparison requires matched tokenisation and matched endpoint convention. Panel (5 models, study num_samples=200): straightening_ratio 0.0431 / 0.0395 / 0.0517 / 0.0715 / 0.0409 and curvature_slope -0.0912 / -0.1019 / -0.0778 / -0.1035 / -0.1087 for distilgpt2 / gpt2 / pythia-70m / pythia-160m / gpt2-medium. _meta_last_entry_is_block_output was 1.0 on 5/5, so the deepest point really is a block output in all of them.
github_reason: Executed the released curvature_utils.py (vendored by the prior reviewer at verification_campaign/verdicts/_geometry_trajectory_curvature_codex_round10/curvature_utils.released.py) unchanged: its normalized() sets zero-norm rows to 1 and compute_model_curvature() takes arccos of the dot products of L2-normalised consecutive differences, then means per sentence. I ran it head-to-head with BLME's _trajectory_angles on (a) the mixed-step counterexample, (b) a 60-degree uniform turn at all 8 ladder rungs, and (c) 200 random (T,D) trajectories. Worst per-angle |diff| 2.5375535007e-14; worst mean |diff| 1.5543122345e-15. One DISCLOSED divergence remains: on an EXACTLY zero difference vector the released code emits arccos(0)=pi/2 (its l2==0 -> 1 rule leaves the zero vector zero, so the dot product is 0) while BLME skips the angle. BLME's choice is the defensible one (a zero velocity has no direction) and the case does not arise on real activations, but it is a difference from the reference and is not documented.
paper_reason: Hosseini & Fedorenko 2023 (arXiv:2311.04930) Fig. S6 reports the stochastic Gaussian baseline peaking at ~120 degrees. That value has an exact closed form for an iid Gaussian trajectory: consecutive difference vectors share -x_{t+1}, so E<v_t,v_{t+1}> = -D and E||v||^2 = 2D, giving cos = -1/2 and an angle of exactly 120 degrees. BLME returns 119.999582 degrees over 4,000 trajectories of length 6-19 in D=1600 (relative error 3.4824e-06, consistent with Monte-Carlo error at that n). No trained-model figure value is tabulated in the paper for direct reproduction.
confounds_reason: The angle itself is dimension-invariant by construction (0.0 rad change under isometric embedding from D=2 to D=1600), which rules out a mechanical d_model proxy, and straightening_ratio is essentially uncorrelated with size on my 5-model panel (Spearman rho with parameter count -0.200, with d_model -0.447). curvature_slope is the exception: rho = -1.000 with parameter count, -0.949 with n_layers and -0.894 with d_model over distilgpt2 / gpt2 / pythia-70m / pythia-160m / gpt2-medium (values -0.0912 / -0.1019 / -0.0778 / -0.1035 / -0.1087). n=5 with depth taking only three values cannot separate a size effect from a real one, but the slope is the output to watch, and it is also the one whose depth normalisation I measured as only approximate (see normalized_ok). The mechanism most likely to matter is not width but trajectory sampling density: the same circle read at 6 vs 60 points gives 72.000 vs 6.102 degrees in BLME and in the released code alike, so tokenizer granularity and passage-length distribution enter directly.

PRECISION, CODE: _pooled_layer_curvature (trajectory_curvature.py:159-161) does chunk.detach().float().cpu().numpy() before the float64 promotion on the next line, so a float64 input tensor is narrowed to float32 first. Harmless in production (HF hidden states are fp32/bf16, so .float() is a no-op or an upcast) but it is the same narrow-then-promote ordering that safe_svdvals was explicitly fixed for.

NORMALIZED VARIANT: curvature_slope removes the 1/(L-1) scaling exactly but is only approximately depth-normalised. Holding a fixed continuous profile and resampling it, the slope drifts -0.120000000000 (L=4) -> -0.133566433566 (L=12) -> -0.141684759010 (L=48), an 18.1% change from a pure change of sampling density; and appending 20 flat layers to [2.1,1.7,1.6,2.0] moves it -0.120 -> +0.116 (sign reversal), so it is not invariant to where in depth the straightening happens.
